items.title: Verifying that filtering works
items.text:
With a phone connected and in an AdGuard group:

# From the phone (or any peer in the group), you should see an answer of 0.0.0.0:
dig @10.100.0.1 doubleclick.net

# On the server, the redirect rules should list the phone's tunnel address:
iptables -t nat -S TUNGARD_DNS

Then open /adguard-ui/ → Query Log to watch the blocked lookups arrive in real time.

items.title: Admin Panel
items.text:
Manage peers, settings, backups and the API from the browser.

The TunGuard Admin Panel provides access to server settings, authentication, API access, backups, and peer management.

items.title: Dashboard Login
items.text:
Change the username and password used to access the TunGuard Admin Panel.

Go to:

Settings → Dashboard Login

Changes take effect immediately.

items.title: API Key
items.text:
TunGuard provides an API key for authenticating API requests.

Go to:

Settings → API Key

From here you can:

  • Generate an API key
  • View the current API key
  • Revoke the current API key
  • Generate a new API key

Once an API key is revoked, applications using the old key can no longer authenticate.

API requests can authenticate using either:

X-API-Key: YOUR_API_KEY

or:

Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY

Keep your API key private. Anyone with the key can access the API according to the permissions provided by TunGuard.

items.title: Backup & Restore
items.text:
TunGuard can back up its persistent configuration so it can be restored later.

Go to:

Settings → Backup & Restore

items.title: Download Backup
items.text:
Download a backup containing the persistent TunGuard state.

Backups can be used to recover a server or move an existing TunGuard installation to another server.

items.title: Restore Backup
items.text:
A backup can be imported into a new TunGuard installation.

This is useful when moving from one server to another.

The restored state can include:

  • Server configuration
  • WireGuard server key
  • Peer configuration
  • Dashboard credentials
  • API key
  • Other persistent TunGuard data

Server Key

If the restored backup contains a different WireGuard server private key, existing peers will need updated configurations.

items.title: Moving TunGuard to a New Server
items.text:
To move TunGuard to another server:

  1. Download a backup from the old server.
  2. Install TunGuard on the new server.
  3. Open Settings → Backup & Restore.
  4. Import the backup.
  5. Restart TunGuard if required.
  6. Update the server address in client configurations if the server's public address changed.

The backup does not replace the TunGuard binary or systemd service configuration.

items.title: Peer Management
items.text:
Peer management is available from the Peers section.

Administrators can:

  • Create peers
  • Edit peers
  • Enable or disable peers
  • Generate peer configurations
  • Display peer QR codes
  • Add existing WireGuard keys
  • Remove peers

See Edit Peer for the available peer settings.

items.title: Policy Groups
items.text:
Policy groups are available from the Policy section. Each group holds a set of devices and its own set of rules:

Rule Allows Inter-device traffic Devices in this group to reach each other P2P mesh Devices in this group to be punched together TCP relay Port mappings (TRP proxies) onto these devices WireGuard access Internet access out through the tunnel AdGuard DNS filtering Port-53 DNS of this group's devices is redirected to the embedded AdGuard Home

See AdGuard DNS Filtering for what the AdGuard switch does.

Every rule starts off, and every device is in exactly one group. Devices in no custom group are in Default, whose rules apply until you change them.

Administrators can:

  • Create, rename, edit and delete groups
  • Move devices between groups, including back to Default
  • See how many packets the filter has dropped for inter-device and internet access

Groups do not reach into each other

Inter-device traffic stays inside one group. Opening it on one group does not open any other group, and a device in Default cannot reach a device in a custom group. Devices that need to talk to each other belong in the same group.

items.title: Server Settings
items.text:
TunGuard provides settings for configuring the WireGuard server and its network.

Common settings include:

  • WireGuard interface
  • WireGuard listen port
  • VPN address
  • VPN subnet
  • MTU
  • External network interface
  • Dashboard/API listener
  • SSH Gateway

Changes to networking settings can affect connected peers. Make sure client configurations match the server configuration after making changes.

items.title: SSH Gateway
items.text:
The optional SSH Gateway turns TunGuard into a jump host so administrators can reach devices connected through TunGuard without exposing SSH on them.

The full story — enabling it, jumping to a peer, the browser SSH terminal, and the built-in ssh client — is in the SSH Access guide. As a quick start, with the gateway enabled the default port is 2222 and you connect with:

ssh -J admin@YOUR_SERVER_IP:2222 root@10.100.0.2

items.title: Domains & HTTPS
items.text: TunGuard can publish an internal service on a public domain with automatic Let's Encrypt HTTPS — in front of a TRP mapping or a tunneled WireGuard service. Manage mappings from the Domains page, the API, or the console. See Domains & HTTPS Proxy.

items.title: AdGuard DNS Filtering
items.text: A managed AdGuard Home can filter DNS for devices in an AdGuard-enabled policy group. It starts automatically, its DNS service binds to the tunnel address, and protected devices are redirected to it on the server — moving a device into the group takes effect immediately. See AdGuard DNS Filtering.

items.title: Security
items.text:
The Admin Panel controls access to sensitive TunGuard functionality.

Administrators should:

  • Change the default dashboard credentials after installation.
  • Protect API keys.
  • Revoke API keys that are no longer trusted.
  • Keep backups in a secure location.
  • Use HTTPS when exposing the dashboard through a public network.

items.title: API Reference
items.text:
peers mesh domains

Every dashboard action has an HTTP API equivalent.

TunGuard provides an HTTP API for managing the VPN server, its peers, and the P2P mesh.

The API is available under:

http://YOUR_SERVER_IP:9000/api

items.title: Endpoint overview
items.text:
Endpoint Method Auth Purpose /api/health GET None Liveness check /api/status GET Either Server and peer status /api/system GET Either Host metrics /api/server_key GET Either Server public key and port /api/configure POST Either Change key or listen port at runtime /api/peers GET Either List peers /api/peer/add POST Either Add an existing public key /api/peer/remove POST Either Remove a peer /api/peer/config POST Either Re-render a peer's configuration /api/peer/generate-config POST Either Create a peer with a new key pair /api/version GET Either Version and update check /api/update POST Either Replace the binary and restart /api/backup/download GET Either Download a data directory backup /api/backup/restore POST Either Restore a backup /api/peer-monitor/events GET Either Peer event history /api/peer-monitor/state GET Either Latest peer metrics /api/ws/ssh GET Either WebSocket SSH session /api/auth/status GET Dashboard Current user, default-credential warning /api/web/credentials POST Dashboard Change dashboard password /api/key GET Dashboard Read the current API key /api/key/regenerate POST Dashboard Issue a new API key /api/mesh/* Various Either P2P mesh /api/trp/* Various Either TCP relay proxies /api/policy/* Various Either Policy groups /api/domains GET Either List domain mappings and proxy status /api/domains/status GET Either Domain proxy serving mode /api/domain/add POST Either Add a domain mapping /api/domain/update POST Either Update a domain mapping /api/domain/remove POST Either Remove a domain mapping /api/adguard GET Either AdGuard status /api/adguard/start POST Either Start the managed AdGuard Home /api/adguard/stop POST Either Stop the managed AdGuard Home /api/adguard/config GET/POST Either Effective ADGUARD_* configuration /adguard-ui/ GET Dashboard Reverse proxy to the AdGuard web UI

"Either" means the dashboard login or an API key. "Dashboard" means the login is required and an API key is rejected.

items.title: Authentication
items.text:
All /api/* endpoints require authentication except /api/health.

Most endpoints accept either the dashboard credentials or an API key. A small group of credential and key management endpoints accept only the dashboard login — see Credential and key management.

Endpoint group Accepted credentials Most /api/*, all /api/mesh/*, all /api/trp/* Dashboard login or API key /api/auth/status, /api/web/credentials, /api/key, /api/key/regenerate Dashboard login only /api/health, /api/login, /api/logout None

items.title: Dashboard Authentication
items.text:
The browser dashboard signs in through an HTML form and a session cookie. For scripts, use HTTP Basic Authentication:

curl -u admin:PASSWORD http://localhost:9000/api/status

POST /api/login with a JSON {"username":...,"password":...} body establishes the same session the browser gets and returns the cookie, and POST /api/logout clears it. Neither is needed for the Basic-auth flow above. If the server is still on the shipped admin / tanguard login, signing in reports must_change: true and the dashboard forces you to set your own login before you can use it.

items.title: API Key
items.text:
Generate or rotate the API key from:

Settings → API Key

You can also generate one from the terminal using dashboard authentication:

curl -X POST \
  -u admin:PASSWORD \
  http://localhost:9000/api/key/regenerate

The response contains the new API key.

Store it securely:

API_KEY="REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_KEY"

Use the key with the X-API-Key header:

curl \
  -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  http://localhost:9000/api/status

The API key can also be sent using:

Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY

Why the API key cannot manage itself

An API key is deliberately rejected by /api/key and /api/key/regenerate. A leaked key can therefore be rotated, but only by someone who also has the dashboard password. This is the difference between a key that can be neutralised and one that cannot.

items.title: GET /api/health
items.text:
Returns the health status of the TunGuard server.

This endpoint does not require authentication and exposes no sensitive information.

curl http://localhost:9000/api/health

This endpoint is suitable for uptime checks and load balancers.

items.title: GET /api/status
items.text:
Returns information about the TunGuard server and WireGuard status.

curl \
  -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  http://localhost:9000/api/status

items.title: GET /api/server_key
items.text:
Returns the WireGuard server public key.

curl \
  -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  http://localhost:9000/api/server_key

items.title: GET /api/system
items.text:
Returns host metrics: hostname, OS, kernel, CPU model and core count, CPU utilisation, load averages, process counts, uptime, memory, disk usage for the data directory, and per-interface network counters.

curl \
  -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  http://localhost:9000/api/system

Response:

{
  "hostname": "vpn-01",
  "os": "Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm)",
  "kernel": "6.1.0-18-amd64",
  "cpu_model": "Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8375C CPU @ 2.90GHz",
  "cpu_cores": 4,
  "cpu_percent": 7.4,
  "load": [0.11, 0.08, 0.02],
  "uptime": 841203,
  "processes": { "total": 214, "running": 3 },
  "memory": { "total": 8123456, "used": 3910553, "percent": 48.1 },
  "disk": { "total": 41153856, "used": 12451840, "percent": 30.2 },
  "network": []
}

disk reflects the partition holding DATA_DIR, not the whole filesystem.

items.title: POST /api/configure
items.text:
Applies runtime changes without a restart. Both parameters are optional; send whichever you need.

curl -X POST \
  -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "private_key": "REPLACE_WITH_64_CHAR_HEX_PRIVATE_KEY",
    "listen_port": 51820
  }' \
  http://localhost:9000/api/configure

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Parameter Required Description private_key No New WireGuard server private key. Must be valid hex listen_port No New WireGuard listen port. Recorded, but a restart is required to apply it

If a new private_key is accepted, it is written to DATA_DIR/server_private.key with mode 0600, and the response includes the resulting server_public_key.

Rotating the server key invalidates every peer config

Peer configurations embed the server public key. After rotating, previously issued
client configurations stop working and must be regenerated with `/api/peer/config`.

Not available in mesh-only mode

With -mesh-only there is no WireGuard interface to reconfigure, so this endpoint must not be used. Use the mesh and configuration file endpoints instead.

items.title: GET /api/peers
items.text:
Returns the peers currently configured on the TunGuard server.

curl \
  -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  http://localhost:9000/api/peers

items.title: POST /api/peer/add
items.text:
Adds a peer using an existing WireGuard public key.

curl -X POST \
  -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "public_key": "PEER_PUBKEY_HEX",
    "allowed_ip": "10.100.0.2/32",
    "device_name": "my-device"
  }' \
  http://localhost:9000/api/peer/add

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Parameter Required Description public_key Yes WireGuard public key of the peer. Must be valid hex allowed_ip Yes VPN address assigned to the peer, in CIDR form. Must not already be assigned device_name No Label used to identify the peer in the dashboard

Returns 409 if the public key is already registered, or if allowed_ip is already assigned to another peer.

items.title: POST /api/peer/generate-config
items.text:
Creates a new peer and generates its WireGuard client configuration.

TunGuard generates the client's WireGuard key pair. Nothing is required — every parameter has a default:

curl -X POST \
  -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "device_name": "my-phone",
    "server_host": "vpn.example.com"
  }' \
  http://localhost:9000/api/peer/generate-config

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Parameter Required Default Description device_name No — Label used to identify the peer device_id No — Identifier stored with the peer record server_host No Host of the request Public hostname or IP clients use to reach TunGuard allowed_ip No Next free address VPN address to assign. Must not already be assigned dns No 1.1.1.1 DNS server written into the generated configuration

Leaving server_host out uses the Host header of the request, so the generated endpoint matches however you reached the server — but set it explicitly if you want a different public hostname in the output.

The response contains the generated client configuration, including the peer's private key. Treat it as a secret.

items.title: POST /api/peer/config
items.text:
Generates the complete WireGuard configuration for an existing peer.

This is useful for re-downloading or re-rendering a configuration for a peer created using /api/peer/generate-config.

curl -X POST \
  -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "public_key": "PEER_PUBKEY_HEX",
    "server_host": "vpn.example.com"
  }' \
  http://localhost:9000/api/peer/config

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Parameter Required Description public_key Yes WireGuard public key of the peer server_host Yes Public hostname or IP address clients use to reach TunGuard

For peers created using generate-config, the returned configuration can include the client's private key.

Treat generated configurations as sensitive.

items.title: POST /api/peer/remove
items.text:
Removes a peer from TunGuard.

curl -X POST \
  -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "public_key": "PEER_PUBKEY_HEX"
  }' \
  http://localhost:9000/api/peer/remove

items.title: Parameters
items.text: Parameter Required Description public_key Yes WireGuard public key of the peer to remove

items.title: Credential and key management
items.text: These four endpoints all require the dashboard login. An API key is rejected, so a leaked key can always be rotated by someone who holds the password.

items.title: GET /api/auth/status
items.text:
Returns the authenticated username and whether the server is still on default credentials. Used by the dashboard to decide whether to force a password change.

curl -u admin:PASSWORD http://localhost:9000/api/auth/status

{
  "authenticated": true,
  "username": "admin",
  "must_change": true
}

must_change is true only when no credentials have been stored yet and the configured username and password are still admin / tanguard.

items.title: POST /api/web/credentials
items.text:
Changes the dashboard username and password.

curl -X POST \
  -u admin:tanguard \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "username": "alice",
    "password": "a-long-passphrase",
    "confirm_password": "a-long-passphrase"
  }' \
  http://localhost:9000/api/web/credentials

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Parameter Required Description username Yes New dashboard username. Whitespace is trimmed; cannot be empty password Yes New password. Minimum 8 characters confirm_password Yes Must match password exactly

Changing the password invalidates every existing session and API key, so update your clients at the same time.

items.title: GET /api/key
items.text:
Returns the current API key, if one exists.

curl -u admin:PASSWORD http://localhost:9000/api/key

{
  "exists": true,
  "key": "REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_KEY",
  "created_at": "2026-01-14T09:31:07Z"
}

When no key has been generated yet, exists is false and key is an empty string. created_at is only present when a key exists.

items.title: POST /api/key/regenerate
items.text:
Creates a new API key and invalidates the previous key.

Dashboard authentication is required for this endpoint.

curl -X POST \
  -u admin:PASSWORD \
  http://localhost:9000/api/key/regenerate

The response contains the new key and its creation timestamp. The previous key stops working immediately, so update any applications or automation that relied on it.

items.title: GET /api/version
items.text:
Returns the running version, the latest published release, and update metadata. The version check runs in the background; results are cached.

curl -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" http://localhost:9000/api/version

{
  "current_version": "v1.2.0",
  "latest_version": "v1.3.0",
  "update_available": true,
  "download_url": "https://github.com/TunGuard/tanguard-binary/releases/download/v1.3.0/tanguard-linux-amd64",
  "release_notes": "https://api.github.com/repos/TunGuard/tanguard-binary/releases/latest",
  "release_url": "https://github.com/TunGuard/tanguard-binary/releases/tag/v1.3.0",
  "arch": "amd64",
  "last_checked": "2026-01-14T09:00:00Z"
}

Add ?refresh=1 to query GitHub immediately instead of returning the cached result:

curl -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" "http://localhost:9000/api/version?refresh=1"

items.title: POST /api/update
items.text:
Downloads a new binary, replaces the running executable, and restarts the process with the same arguments.

curl -X POST \
  -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"download_url": "https://github.com/TunGuard/tanguard-binary/releases/download/v1.3.0/tanguard-linux-amd64"}' \
  http://localhost:9000/api/update

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Parameter Required Description download_url Yes URL of the replacement binary

This endpoint replaces the running binary

/api/update fetches download_url with no checksum or signature check, writes it over the running executable, and re-execs it. Anything able to call this endpoint can install arbitrary code as your server user.

Prefer downloading the release yourself, verifying it, and restarting through your process supervisor. If you do use this endpoint, only ever pass a download_url you obtained directly from the project's own releases, and never from a redirecting shortener or mirror.

The download is capped at 256 MB, and a payload under 100 KB is rejected. A second concurrent call returns 409 while an update is already in progress.

items.title: GET /api/backup/download
items.text:
Streams a .tar.gz backup of the data directory. The archive contains a manifest.json recording the tool, version, creation time, and data directory path.

curl \
  -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -o tanguard-backup.tar.gz \
  http://localhost:9000/api/backup/download

items.title: POST /api/backup/restore
items.text:
Restores a backup produced by /api/backup/download. Send the archive as a multipart form field named backup.

curl -X POST \
  -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -F "backup=@tanguard-backup.tar.gz" \
  http://localhost:9000/api/backup/restore

Back up before you restore

Restore overwrites the current data directory. Take a fresh download first, and do
not restore while peers are connected.

A backup contains peer private keys and the stored API key. Anyone holding the file
can impersonate your peers and read server credentials. Keep it encrypted at rest.

items.title: Peer monitoring
items.text: These endpoints expose the peer handshakes the dashboard charts. They are registered only when the peer monitor is running, and are absent in -mesh-only mode, where the responses are 404.

items.title: GET /api/peer-monitor/events
items.text:
Returns recorded peer events as a JSON array.

curl -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" http://localhost:9000/api/peer-monitor/events

[
  { "t": "2026-01-14T09:31:07Z", "peer": "a1b2c3d4", "event": "handshake", "detail": "" },
  { "t": "2026-01-14T09:34:12Z", "peer": "e5f6a7b8", "event": "deferred", "detail": "handshake timeout" }
]

items.title: Query parameters
items.text:
Parameter Description since RFC 3339 timestamp. Returns only events strictly after it. Invalid values are ignored peer Public key prefix. Returns only events for that peer 
curl -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  "http://localhost:9000/api/peer-monitor/events?peer=a1b2c3d4&since=2026-01-14T09:00:00Z"

This is a polling endpoint, not a stream — it returns the current buffer and closes.

items.title: GET /api/peer-monitor/state
items.text:
Returns a snapshot of the most recent metrics per peer, keyed by shortened public key.

curl -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" http://localhost:9000/api/peer-monitor/state

{
  "a1b2c3d4": {
    "handshake": 1768382345,
    "endpoint": "198.51.100.24:4711",
    "txBytes": 184432,
    "rxBytes": 229104
  }
}

handshake is a Unix timestamp of the last completed handshake, or 0 if none has happened yet.

items.title: GET /api/ws/ssh
items.text:
Upgrades the connection to a WebSocket and opens a pseudo-terminal onto the host, which is how the dashboard's SSH Gateway works. In a browser this must be requested as a WebSocket; it cannot be called with a plain curl request.

Credentials are taken from the Host header in the form user:password@host:port, and forwarded to the target host. A failure to connect is reported in-band over the socket rather than as an HTTP status.

items.title: Example: Automation
items.text:
A simple script can use an API key to retrieve peer information:

#!/bin/sh

API_KEY="REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_KEY"
API="http://localhost:9000"

curl \
  -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  "$API/api/peers"

items.title: Example: Add a Peer
items.text:
#!/bin/sh

API_KEY="REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_KEY"
API="http://localhost:9000"

curl -X POST \
  -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "public_key": "PEER_PUBKEY_HEX",
    "allowed_ip": "10.100.0.2/32",
    "device_name": "customer-device"
  }' \
  "$API/api/peer/add"

items.title: P2P Mesh
items.text:
The P2P mesh is driven by endpoints under /api/mesh/*. They use the same authentication as the rest of /api/*, and they answer whenever the control plane is running — in a normal server start and under -mesh-only alike.

Mutating calls are POST with a JSON body. A GET on one of those returns 405.

API_KEY="REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_KEY"
H="X-API-Key: $API_KEY"
JSON="Content-Type: application/json"
API="http://localhost:9000"

When the mesh is disabled

With MESH_ENABLED=false the control plane is never started and every endpoint below returns 503 tun control plane is disabled. Under -mesh-only the process refuses to start at all. See P2P Control Plane.

items.title: Nodes and Groups
items.text:
A node is a client allowed onto the mesh. Nodes that share a PSK form a group, and a group auto-meshes: every online member is punched to every other member. A node added without a PSK gets a unique one. Every node/add response returns the generated psk — save it, it is the device's join credential.

# Mesh state: enabled, node/group counts, listen addresses
curl -H "$H" "$API/api/mesh/status"

# List nodes. PSKs are masked; add ?show_psk=1 to reveal them
curl -H "$H" "$API/api/mesh/nodes"
curl -H "$H" "$API/api/mesh/nodes?show_psk=1"

# Devices bucketed by shared PSK, with per-group link counts
curl -H "$H" "$API/api/mesh/groups"

# Every direct and relayed link between nodes
curl -H "$H" "$API/api/mesh/links"

GET /api/mesh/nodes returns one object per node:

Field Description id The node handle every other call needs name Label you chose at enrollment psk The group key (masked unless show_psk=1) device_id The client's own stable identity, reported on connect online Whether the control channel is currently up control_ip Address the control channel came from relay_ep Public UDP endpoint registered at the hub relay_seen When that endpoint was last refreshed peers Number of peers this node holds direct_peers How many of those are direct tested_peers How many of those answered a link test connected_for How long the node has been connected

A node with a relay_ep but no direct_peers is the one to investigate: discovery worked and the hole punch did not.

GET /api/mesh/links returns one object per link:

Field Description from / to Node ids of the two ends online Whether the far node is connected endpoint Public endpoint the punch is aimed at direct A punch landed and the peer answered tested A link test completed on this link rtt_ms Round trip the client measured, in milliseconds direct_since When the link first went direct

direct and tested answer different questions. direct is the punch: one packet arrived, once. tested is the client's own round trip to the peer — a small packet it sent that the peer echoed back — so direct with tested false is a link that punched and then went quiet, which is what the dashboard shows as no answer.

# Add a node. Omit "psk" to have one generated.
# A "name" is only a label - it is NOT a unique key, and duplicates are allowed.
curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/mesh/node/add" \
  -d '{"name":"edge-a"}'

# Add a node into an existing group
curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/mesh/node/add" \
  -d '{"name":"edge-b","psk":"shared-group-key"}'

# Remove a node entirely, or just reset it (clears its link state, keeps the record)
curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/mesh/node/remove" \
  -d '{"id":"NODE_ID"}'
curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/mesh/node/reset" \
  -d '{"id":"NODE_ID"}'

Removing a node leaves its proxies behind

node/remove does not clean up the node's TCP relays. Remove those with /api/trp/proxy/remove first, or they keep holding their listeners.

items.title: Direct Paths
items.text:
Nodes in the same group are punched to each other automatically, so these calls are for forcing a re-punch, forcing a group back onto the relay, or taking nodes off the mesh.

p2p/connect needs both nodes online — an offline or unknown id returns 400 node offline. Two nodes whose devices sit in different policy groups cannot be punched together and the call is refused with 400 policy groups are isolated: a direct path never passes through the server, so it is enforced at the point the link is created. Put both devices in one group with allow_inter_device on to link them.

# Force an immediate direct path between two nodes
curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/mesh/p2p/connect" \
  -d '{"a":"NODE_ID_A","b":"NODE_ID_B"}'

# Re-punch a whole group. "group" is the PSK.
curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/mesh/p2p/mesh" \
  -d '{"group":"shared-group-key"}'

# Clear a group's peer table and punch targets
curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/mesh/p2p/mesh" \
  -d '{"group":"shared-group-key","enable":false}'

"enable": false clears the server-side peer table and tells every member to drop its punch targets. It is not a persistent "relay only" mode: each client re-learns the same peers from the next rendezvous reply within a few seconds and resumes punching.

items.title: Rendezvous Hub
items.text:
Attach a node to the relay hub, or detach it. Both need the node connected; an offline or unknown id returns 400 node offline.

curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/mesh/relay/join" \
  -d '{"id":"NODE_ID"}'
curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/mesh/relay/leave" \
  -d '{"id":"NODE_ID"}'

Leaving drops only that node's P2P work. A full reset would also tear down its TCP relay sessions, which is not what leaving the mesh should do.

To manage the relay circuits by hand — pin a relayed path, or drop every link leaving a node:

curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/mesh/relay/link" \
  -d '{"src":"NODE_ID_A","dst":"NODE_ID_B"}'
curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/mesh/relay/unlink" \
  -d '{"src":"NODE_ID_A"}'

These are for overriding the automatic behaviour. Left alone, the server keeps a relay circuit for every pair it attempts to punch, so a link that cannot go direct still carries traffic.

relay/unlink removes the fallback

Dropping a node's relay circuits leaves it with no path for any link that fails to go direct. Use it to isolate a node while debugging, not to pin traffic onto the relay — direct and relayed paths are maintained together, and there is no switch between them.

items.title: TCP Relay (TRP)
items.text:
A TRP proxy listens on the server and forwards each connection to target_ip:target_port on the target node over its mesh path.

Leave bind_port as an empty string to let the OS pick a free port — the chosen port comes back as bind_port and in public_url. "0" is rejected; only an empty string means auto-assign. target_port is always required and always numeric.

# List proxies, with live connection counts
curl -H "$H" "$API/api/trp/proxies"

# Auto-assigned listen port, forwarding to port 8022 on the node
curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/trp/proxy/add" \
  -d '{"node_id":"NODE_ID","bind_port":"","target_port":"8022"}'

# Fixed listen port and an explicit target address
curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/trp/proxy/add" \
  -d '{"node_id":"NODE_ID","bind_ip":"0.0.0.0","bind_port":"18022","target_ip":"127.0.0.1","target_port":"8022"}'

# Remove a proxy
curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/trp/proxy/remove" \
  -d '{"id":"PROXY_ID"}'

items.title: Mesh Errors
items.text:
Failures are JSON with an error field, so scripts can branch on them:

Status Meaning 400 Bad request — id required, node_id required, unknown group, node offline, policy groups are isolated, port out of range, or malformed JSON 401 Missing or invalid dashboard login / API key 404 No such node, proxy, or binding 405 GET used on a POST-only route 503 Mesh control plane not running — set MESH_ENABLED=true (the default)

items.title: Mesh End to End
items.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
API_KEY="REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_KEY"
API="http://localhost:9000"
field() { python3 -c "import json,sys;print(json.load(sys.stdin)['$1'])"; }

# Enroll a device and keep the id and PSK it returns
ADDED="$(curl -sS -X POST -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" "$API/api/mesh/node/add" \
  -d '{"name":"edge-a"}')"
NODE_ID="$(printf '%s' "$ADDED" | field id)"
PSK="$(printf '%s' "$ADDED" | field psk)"
echo "run on the device:  tun YOUR_SERVER_IP $PSK"

# Expose a service running on that node
PROXY="$(curl -sS -X POST -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" "$API/api/trp/proxy/add" \
  -d "{\"node_id\":\"$NODE_ID\",\"bind_port\":\"\",\"target_port\":\"8022\"}")"
echo "reachable at $(printf '%s' "$PROXY" | field public_url)"

# Tear down
curl -sS -X POST -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" "$API/api/trp/proxy/remove" \
  -d "{\"id\":\"$(printf '%s' "$PROXY" | field id)\"}"
curl -sS -X POST -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" "$API/api/mesh/node/remove" \
  -d "{\"id\":\"$NODE_ID\"}"

items.title: Policy Groups API
items.text:
A policy group is a set of devices with its own rules. Every device the server knows about is in exactly one group, and a device in no custom group is in default. The group decides what a device may reach:

Rule Allows allow_inter_device Traffic to the other devices of the same group allow_p2p_mesh P2P mesh participation allow_trp TCP relay proxies onto the group allow_wg_access Internet access out through the tunnel 
API="http://localhost:9000"
H="X-API-Key: $API_KEY"
JSON="Content-Type: application/json"

# Every group with its members, every known device, and the packet-filter
# drop counters for inter-device and internet traffic
curl -H "$H" "$API/api/policy/groups"

# Create a group. Every omitted rule is OFF, so a new group denies by default
curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/policy/group/create" \
  -d '{"name":"office","allow_inter_device":true,"allow_wg_access":true}'

# Change a group. Omitted rules and an empty name keep their current value,
# so this turns on inter-device traffic without touching the other rules
curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/policy/group/update" \
  -d '{"id":"GROUP_ID","allow_inter_device":true}'

# Delete a group. Its devices fall back to the default group
curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/policy/group/delete" \
  -d '{"id":"GROUP_ID"}'

# Move WireGuard peers into a group, by public key
curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/policy/group/assign" \
  -d '{"id":"GROUP_ID","devices":["PEER_PUBKEY_HEX"]}'

# Move tun-client devices into a group, by device id
curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/policy/group/assign-device" \
  -d '{"id":"GROUP_ID","devices":["DEVICE_ID"]}'

# Send devices back to the default group
curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/policy/group/unassign" \
  -d '{"devices":["PEER_PUBKEY_HEX"]}'
curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/policy/group/unassign-device" \
  -d '{"devices":["DEVICE_ID"]}'

# Replace the whole policy in one call: groups, peer membership, and device
# membership. Rejected outright if any name names a device the server has
# never seen
curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/policy/apply" \
  -d '{"groups":[{"id":"office","name":"Office","allow_inter_device":true,"allow_wg_access":true}],
       "assign":{"PEER_PUBKEY_HEX":"office"},
       "device_assign":{"DEVICE_ID":"office"}}'

A device is named by public key when it is a WireGuard peer, and by device id when it is a tun-client device with no peer of its own. Sending the wrong identity returns 400 unknown device. group/unassign and group/unassign-device do not need an id — the group id in their response is always default.

Groups are sealed from each other

allow_inter_device opens traffic to the other devices of that group only. It never grants reach into or out of another group, and it does not depend on the other group's own setting: one open side is enough, but only within one group. Before 2.4.2, an open group could reach into a closed one; that leak is fixed, so cross-group traffic now needs the devices to be in the same group — and /api/mesh/p2p/connect refuses such a pair with 400 policy groups are isolated.

items.title: Domains API
items.text:
These endpoints manage the HTTPS domain proxy — a public domain in front of a TRP mapping or a tunneled service, with automatic Let's Encrypt certificates. They use the same credentials as the rest of /api/*, and return 409 domain reverse proxy is disabled when DOMAIN_ENABLED=false.

API="http://localhost:9000"
H="X-API-Key: $API_KEY"
JSON="Content-Type: application/json"

# Every mapping, plus the proxy's serving status
curl -H "$H" "$API/api/domains"

# Proxy status alone: mode, webserver, ports
curl -H "$H" "$API/api/domains/status"

items.title: GET /api/domains
items.text: Returns { domains: [...], status: {...} }. Each domain includes its id, domain name, backend, target, enabled flag, and timestamps.

items.title: GET /api/domains/status
items.text:
Returns the serving mode and the addresses in use:

Field Description enabled Whether the proxy is enabled mode builtin, external, idle, or blocked webserver Detected webserver (nginx, apache, caddy, traefik) owner_80 / owner_443 Process holding ports 80/443, if any http_port / https_port Public HTTP/HTTPS ports challenge_port Loopback ACME challenge port count Number of configured mappings

items.title: POST /api/domain/add
items.text:
Create a mapping. Pass either a trp backend with proxy_ref, or a wg backend with target_ip and target_port:

# Behind an existing TRP mapping
curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/domain/add" \
  -d '{"domain":"app.example.com","backend":"trp","proxy_ref":"3"}'

# Behind a tunneled WireGuard service
curl -X POST -H "$H" -H "$JSON" "$API/api/domain/add" \
  -d '{"domain":"api.example.com","backend":"wg","target_ip":"10.100.0.2","target_port":8080}'

enabled defaults to true. The response includes the generated domain id.

items.title: POST /api/domain/update
items.text: Update a mapping by id. Send only the fields you want to change. enabled: false pauses the mapping without deleting it.

items.title: POST /api/domain/remove
items.text: Remove a mapping by id. Returns 404 if it does not exist.

items.title: AdGuard API
items.text:
These endpoints manage the embedded AdGuard Home instance used for DNS filtering. They use the same credentials as the rest of /api/*.

# Status: enabled, running, and the web UI address
curl -H "$H" "$API/api/adguard"

The response is:

{
  "enabled": true,
  "running": true,
  "web": "http://127.0.0.1:1116"
}

items.title: POST /api/adguard/start / POST /api/adguard/stop
items.text: Start or stop the managed AdGuard Home. Both rebuild the tunnel DNS redirect rules: starting AdGuard enables redirecting AdGuard-group peers to it, stopping it clears every redirect. Returns 409 when AdGuard is disabled.

items.title: GET/POST /api/adguard/config
items.text: Reads the effective configuration — enabled, dns, web, upstream, family, adult — mirroring the ADGUARD_* environment variables.

items.title: /adguard-ui/ (dashboard login only)
items.text:
A reverse proxy to the AdGuard web UI on its loopback port. Requires the dashboard login (an API key is rejected) and returns 503 while AdGuard is not running:

http://YOUR_SERVER_IP:9000/adguard-ui/

items.title: API Security
items.text:
API keys provide access to protected TunGuard API endpoints. Keep them private and do not commit them to source control.

If a key is exposed, rotate it immediately from:

Settings → API Key

or:

curl -X POST \
  -u admin:PASSWORD \
  http://localhost:9000/api/key/regenerate

For production deployments, protect the dashboard and API with HTTPS when they are exposed over an untrusted network.

An API key is a broad credential: it can add and remove peers, read and restore backups, and replace the server binary via /api/update. Scope it like a password, and prefer issuing short-lived credentials from a provisioning job over a long-lived shared key.

Two endpoints deserve particular attention:

  • /api/update fetches an arbitrary URL and overwrites the running executable. Only point it at releases you obtained directly from the project's own release page.
  • /api/ws/ssh opens an interactive shell to the host. Anyone who can reach the API can reach the machine's SSH credentials, so keep the API off untrusted networks.

Both are reasons to terminate TLS in front of the API and to keep the default dashboard credentials from surviving first boot.

items.title: CLI
items.text: TunGuard can be managed directly from the command line or through systemd when installed as a service.

items.title: Install
items.text:
Install TunGuard on a Linux server with:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TunGuard/get/main/installer.sh | bash

The installer installs TunGuard as a systemd service and starts it automatically.

items.title: Service Management
items.text:
Check the service status:

sudo systemctl status tanguard

Start TunGuard:

sudo systemctl start tanguard

Stop TunGuard:

sudo systemctl stop tanguard

Restart TunGuard:

sudo systemctl restart tanguard

Enable TunGuard to start automatically on boot:

sudo systemctl enable tanguard

items.title: Logs
items.text:
View the TunGuard service logs:

sudo journalctl -u tanguard

Follow the logs in real time:

sudo journalctl -u tanguard -f

Show logs from the current boot:

sudo journalctl -u tanguard -b

Show the most recent logs:

sudo journalctl -u tanguard -n 100

items.title: Reset Dashboard Credentials
items.text:
If you forget the dashboard username or password, stop TunGuard first:

sudo systemctl stop tanguard

Run the reset command:

sudo ./tanguard --reset

The reset restores:

Username: admin
Password: tanguard

Start TunGuard again:

sudo systemctl start tanguard

The complete procedure is:

sudo systemctl stop tanguard
sudo ./tanguard --reset
sudo systemctl start tanguard

This resets the stored dashboard login without removing the configured peers or other persistent TunGuard data.

items.title: Manual Run
items.text:
TunGuard can also be started directly from the command line.

sudo ./tanguard

Enable the web dashboard when running manually:

sudo ./tanguard -web

Enable the SSH Gateway:

sudo ./tanguard -ssh

Enable both:

sudo ./tanguard -web -ssh

When using the systemd service installed by the installer, these options are configured through the service configuration rather than being required for normal operation.

items.title: SSH Gateway
items.text:
The optional SSH Gateway allows you to reach devices connected to TunGuard through the VPN.

The default SSH Gateway port is:

2222

For example, to connect to a WireGuard peer at 10.100.0.2:

ssh -J admin@YOUR_SERVER_IP:2222 root@10.100.0.2

The SSH Gateway uses the TunGuard dashboard credentials for authentication.

The jump host can be used without exposing SSH directly on the VPN device.

See SSH Access for the browser SSH terminal, the built-in ssh client, and the jump command.

items.title: Domains (HTTPS Reverse Proxy)
items.text:
TunGuard can publish a domain with automatic HTTPS in front of a TRP mapping or a tunneled service. Manage mappings from the console:

domain list                                     mappings: domain, backend, target, state
domain add app.example.com --trp 3              behind an existing TRP mapping
domain add api.example.com --wg 10.100.0.2 8080 behind a tunneled WireGuard service
domain update app.example.com --disable         pause without deleting
domain remove app.example.com                   by id or domain name

See Domains & HTTPS Proxy for the full guide.

items.title: AdGuard Home
items.text:
The built-in AdGuard Home can filter DNS for devices in an AdGuard-enabled policy group:

adguard status     state, DNS/Web listen addresses, upstream, adult filter
adguard start      launch the managed AdGuard Home instance
adguard stop       stop it
adguard config     binary, data dir and all ADGUARD_* settings

See AdGuard DNS Filtering for the full guide.

items.title: SSH Gateway With a Custom Port
items.text:
If the SSH Gateway is configured to use another port, specify that port in the jump host:

ssh -J admin@YOUR_SERVER_IP:CUSTOM_PORT root@10.100.0.2

items.title: Check the SSH Gateway
items.text:
Check whether TunGuard is running:

sudo systemctl status tanguard

Then check that the SSH Gateway is listening on port 2222:

sudo ss -lntp | grep 2222

items.title: Check the Dashboard/API
items.text:
The default dashboard and API port is:

9000

Check whether TunGuard is listening:

sudo ss -lntp | grep 9000

The health endpoint can be checked locally with:

curl http://127.0.0.1:9000/api/health

items.title: Check the WireGuard Port
items.text:
The default WireGuard port is:

13231/udp

Check whether TunGuard is listening:

sudo ss -lunp | grep 13231

items.title: Update TunGuard
items.text:
Run the installer again to update an existing installation:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TunGuard/get/main/installer.sh | bash

The installer replaces the TunGuard binary while preserving the existing persistent data and service configuration.

items.title: Backup
items.text:
Create a backup of the TunGuard data directory:

sudo tar -czf ~/tanguard-backup.tar.gz -C /var/lib/tanguard .

The persistent data contains the server key, peer configuration, dashboard credentials, API key, and other TunGuard state.

items.title: Useful Service Commands
items.text:
A quick reference:

# Status
sudo systemctl status tanguard

# Start
sudo systemctl start tanguard

# Stop
sudo systemctl stop tanguard

# Restart
sudo systemctl restart tanguard

# Enable at boot
sudo systemctl enable tanguard

# Follow logs
sudo journalctl -u tanguard -f

# Last 100 log entries
sudo journalctl -u tanguard -n 100

items.title: TunGuard Client
items.text:
One tiny binary, one outbound connection, zero local configuration.

The TunGuard client is a small, fully remote-orchestated binary. It starts in the background, opens one outbound connection to your TunGuard server, identifies itself with a shared key, and then does nothing until the server sends a command.

It is a dumb pipe: no config file to edit, no routes to configure, no service to manage, and no local state beyond two small files. Everything it should be doing is decided by the server.

The client is what joins a P2P mesh.

Not a VPN client

tun does not implement WireGuard, does not create a tun0 interface, and does not give you a VPN. Devices on the Peers page of the dashboard join the VPN with an ordinary WireGuard configuration. Devices on the P2P page run tun and form a direct mesh. The two are independent.

items.title: Install
items.text:
On Linux, macOS, Windows, and Termux, run:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TunGuard/get/main/client.sh | bash

The installer detects the platform and architecture, downloads the matching binary from the TunGuard/client releases, verifies its SHA-256 checksum, and links it as tun.

Platform Installs to Linux, macOS ~/.local/bin/tun Termux / Android $PREFIX/bin/tun Generic Android (adb) you choose the path

If the install directory is not on your PATH, the installer prints the line to add. On Termux that is usually:

export PATH="$PREFIX/bin:$PATH"

Download location on Android

Android's W^X and SELinux policies prevent a binary from being executed off the SD card (/sdcard, /storage/emulated). It has to live in app-private storage or somewhere like Termux's $PREFIX/bin. The installer already handles Termux; for other Android setups, push it yourself:

adb push tun_android_arm64-v8a /data/local/tmp/tun
adb shell chmod +x /data/local/tmp/tun
adb shell /data/local/tmp/tun YOUR_SERVER_IP YOUR_PSK

items.title: Run it
items.text:
tun <control-server-ip> <psk>

For example:

tun 203.0.113.10 secretkey99

The <psk> is the group key from the P2P → Enroll device dialog. Anyone holding it joins your group, so treat it as a credential.

The client double-forks into the background and returns you to the shell. On Windows it stays in the foreground unless TUN_FOREGROUND=1 is set, so run it from a scheduled task or keep the window open.

Once it is running you never need to touch it again. It reconnects on its own if the server goes away, and it re-establishes the mesh after a reboot.

items.title: Check that it is running
items.text:
The client is silent by design, so verify it three ways:

# 1. the process is alive — this is the reliable health check
pgrep -laf tun
# or
ps -ef | grep [t]un

# 2. the control connection to your server:7000 is established
ss -tnp | grep tun        # Linux
netstat -tnp | grep tun   # macOS

# 3. it is connected to the dashboard — check the P2P page on the server

The ESTABLISHED socket is the confirmation that the client is currently talking to the server. Note that the process stays alive even when the control link is down — it reconnects every ~2s, and every ~5s while the server is unreachable — so pgrep is the check that actually tells you something.

To stop it:

pkill -x tun        # by exact process name

The process name is the binary name

If you renamed the binary, use the new name in pgrep and pkill.

items.title: State
items.text:
The client keeps everything it needs in one directory, ~/.tun by default:

# connection  (mode 0600 — holds the shared secret)
server=203.0.113.10
psk=secretkey99

# device_id  (8 hex chars — this node's identity in the mesh)
6bb8a291

device_id is generated once and is what lets a reconnecting device reclaim its record instead of appearing as a stranger. Do not delete this directory — if you do, the node re-registers under a new identity and the server keeps the old record as a ghost until you remove it.

Run the client with no arguments to reuse the saved server and key:

tun

To put the directory somewhere else — useful on a read-only install path — either set the environment variable or pass a third argument:

TUN_STATE_DIR=/var/lib/tun tun
tun 203.0.113.10 secretkey99 /var/lib/tun

Missing directories, including nested ones, are created. Re-running tun <ip> <psk> re-points the client at a new server and rewrites both the state files and the boot hook.

items.title: Survives a reboot
items.text:
On its first successful run as root (or an elevated shell on Windows), the client installs a boot hook for the platform it is on. Each one is best-effort and silently skipped when it does not apply:

Platform Boot hook Linux /etc/systemd/system/tun.service, enabled with systemctl Windows HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\tun Android /data/adb/service.d/tun.sh, which Magisk runs as root at boot

The hook records the absolute path of the binary and the state directory, because it re-runs the client with no arguments and could not otherwise find a non-default state directory.

# check what got installed
systemctl status tun     # Linux
ls -l /data/adb/service.d/tun.sh   # Android

Because boot hooks supervise the process directly, the client skips its double-fork when TUN_FOREGROUND=1 is set. That is what the systemd unit uses; a manual tun <ip> <psk> still backgrounds as before.

items.title: What the client does
items.text:
The client only relays sockets. It never changes routing, never opens a tunnel device, and never writes a config.

Session What the operator sees Control link One outbound TCP connection to server:7000 P2P hub One UDP socket registered with server:7001 P2P peer One UDP socket per peer, with constant keepalive traffic FRP A local listener whose connections are forwarded to the server TRP A TCP pair the server asks the client to pump After reset Every listener and socket is gone; the node is idle

Toggling is seamless. A new command replaces the previous session for that type, and a reset always stops everything.

The protocol

The wire format — command bytes, the 17-byte frame layout, and the status report the client sends upward every five seconds — is documented in P2P Mesh.

items.title: Build from source
items.text:
The client is a single C file with no dependencies beyond libc.

git clone https://github.com/TunGuard/client.git
cd client
make          # builds ./tun for your host

Per-platform targets:

make linux      # static musl builds for x86_64 and arm64
make macos      # x86_64 and arm64
make windows    # MinGW-w64, x86_64 and i686
make android    # NDK, arm64-v8a / armeabi-v7a / x86_64
make release    # everything

Linux binaries are statically linked against musl, so they have no libc dependency at all. macOS uses Apple clang, Windows uses MinGW-w64. Android is built through the NDK and links against bionic, never glibc:

export ANDROID_NDK_HOME=$HOME/Android/Sdk/ndk/27.2.12479018
make android

Android binaries are PIE and dynamically linked against the device's own libc.so. That is deliberate: bionic refuses to run statically linked executables on ARM/ARM64 below API 29, and every device already ships the loader and libc. All Android ABIs target minSdk 21 (Android 5.0+).

Releases for every platform are published on the TunGuard/client releases page, which is what client.sh downloads from.

items.title: Limitations
items.text:
• The PSK is sent in cleartext over the control channel and stored on disk in the state directory. On hostile networks, wrap the control link in a tunnel or encrypt above it. The handshake is always outbound, so NAT and firewalls never block it.
  • Routers are not a target. Consumer router firmware (RouterOS, OpenWrt) is deliberately unsupported: this client relays sockets and never creates a tun0 interface, so sideloading it onto locked-down firmware is not automatable. Point a supported host at the control server instead.
  • BSD is not in the release matrix. Only Linux, macOS, Windows, and Android are built.
  • No state beyond the two files in the state directory. The server stays the single source of truth for what every pipeline should be doing.

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
• P2P Mesh — how the mesh is built, punched, and relayed, and how to drive it from the dashboard or the API.
  • Configuration — the server-side control-plane settings this client connects to.

items.title: General
items.text:
• Name: The name used to identify the peer.
  • Enabled: Whether the peer is allowed to connect to the VPN.

items.title: Address
items.text:
• IPv4: The IPv4 address assigned to the peer.

TunGuard uses the configured VPN subnet to assign peer addresses.

The default VPN subnet is:

10.100.0.0/24

The server uses:

10.100.0.1

and peers are assigned addresses such as:

10.100.0.2
10.100.0.3
10.100.0.4

items.title: Allowed IPs
items.text:
The networks that the peer will route through the VPN.

For example:

0.0.0.0/0, ::/0

routes all IPv4 and IPv6 traffic through TunGuard.

A more specific configuration can be used when the peer should only route selected networks.

items.title: DNS
items.text:
The DNS server that will be configured for the peer.

For example:

1.1.1.1

If the peer belongs to a policy group with AdGuard DNS filtering enabled, the generated profile instead points at the server's own AdGuard (for example 10.100.0.1), so its queries get filtered.

AdGuard protection no longer needs the profile

Since 2.4.17 the server redirects the port-53 DNS of any device in an AdGuard-enabled group, whatever its profile says. A phone generated with DNS = 1.1.1.1 is protected the moment it is moved into an AdGuard group — no re-import — and returns to unfiltered DNS when it is moved back. See AdGuard DNS Filtering.

Android Private DNS

If an Android device has Private DNS set to a specific provider (DNS-over-HTTPS/TLS), its queries are encrypted and bypass the server-side redirect. Set Private DNS to Off or Automatic so the filtered DNS in the WireGuard profile is used.

items.title: Persistent Keepalive
items.text:
The interval, in seconds, at which the peer sends keepalive packets to the TunGuard server.

This can help maintain connections when the peer is behind NAT or a restrictive firewall.

A common value is:

25

items.title: Keys
items.text:
TunGuard uses WireGuard public and private keys for peer authentication.

When creating a peer, TunGuard can generate the required keys automatically.

Existing WireGuard keys can also be added when configuring an existing peer.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
TunGuard generates a standard WireGuard client configuration for each peer.

A generated configuration contains:

[Interface]
PrivateKey = <client-private-key>
Address = 10.100.0.2/32
DNS = 1.1.1.1

[Peer]
PublicKey = <server-public-key>
Endpoint = yourserver:13231
AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0, ::/0
PersistentKeepalive = 25

The configuration can be downloaded, copied, or displayed as a QR code from the dashboard.

items.title: Actions
items.text:
• Save: Save changes made to the peer.
  • Revert: Discard unsaved changes.
  • Delete: Remove the peer from TunGuard.
  • Generate Config: Generate the peer's WireGuard configuration.
  • QR Code: Display the peer configuration as a QR code.

items.title: Domains & HTTPS Proxy
items.text:
DoH :443 DoT :853

Automatic HTTPS on your domain, plus an optional public DoH + DoT resolver.

TunGuard can publish an internal service on a public domain with HTTPS handled automatically. You point a domain at the server and choose the service behind it; TunGuard terminates TLS with a Let's Encrypt certificate and proxies to that service.

The same mapping can also turn a domain into a public DNS resolver that serves DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) and DNS-over-TLS (DoT) backed by the managed AdGuard Home filter. See Serving a public DNS resolver.

The domain proxy is on by default but does nothing until you add a mapping — it binds no ports and makes no certificate request until the first domain is configured. Disable it entirely with DOMAIN_ENABLED=false.

items.title: What a mapping is
items.text:
A domain mapping connects one public hostname to a backend reachable from the server:

Backend Target Typical use TRP (trp) An existing TCP relay (TRP) port mapping A service running on a P2P mesh node, exposed through a TRP mapping WireGuard (wg) IP:port of a tunneled service An app running on a WireGuard peer (or any address the server can reach) DNS (dns) The managed AdGuard Home resolver A public, filtered DoH + DoT resolver (like dns.adguard.com)

Example TRP mapping — publish a node's SSH:

trp add edge-a 18022 127.0.0.1 8022
# returns a mapping id, e.g. "3"

then:

domain add shell.example.com --trp 3

Example WireGuard backend — publish an app on the peer 10.100.0.2:

domain add app.example.com --wg 10.100.0.2 8080

The backend is always spoken to over plain HTTP — TLS is terminated at TunGuard (or the webserver it manages). There is no TLS passthrough. The original Host header is preserved to the backend, and X-Forwarded-For/X-Forwarded-Proto: https are added, so an app that cares about the incoming hostname sees app.example.com.

items.title: HTTPS with Let's Encrypt
items.text:
Certificates come from Let's Encrypt automatically using the HTTP-01 challenge. There is no self-signed mode and no manual certificate files for domains.

For that to work:

  1. Your domain's A (and AAAA, if used) record must point at the server.
  2. Ports 80 and 443 must be reachable on the server.

TunGuard stores certificates under DATA_DIR/domains/certs/<domain>/ and renews them automatically when a certificate is missing or expires within 30 days. It will never request a certificate for a domain that has no mapping, and the built-in proxy returns 404 domain not configured on this server for any other host.

items.title: How traffic is served
items.text:
On the first mapping TunGuard decides how to serve it by looking at the web stack already on the machine:

  • nginx / Apache / Caddy / Traefik — the mapping is written into that server's configuration and reloaded. The config is introspected, never rewritten blindly: stale mappings are cleaned up, and when nginx or Apache is used, the TLS 443 block is only written once the certificate actually exists (a missing cert file would make nginx -t fail).
  • otherwise — the built-in reverse proxy binds DOMAIN_HTTP_PORT: 80 and DOMAIN_HTTPS_PORT: 443 itself, using Go's autocert for HTTPS and a loopback HTTP-01 challenge listener on DOMAIN_CHALLENGE_PORT (default 8100).
  • idle — no mappings configured, nothing is bound.
  • blocked — if an untracked process already holds ports 80/443, the proxy refuses to start rather than fight for them.

With a managed webserver, the ACME challenge for the domain is proxied to the loopback challenge port, so certificate issuance works through the existing web server. After any mapping change or issuance the server configuration is re-written and reloaded.

items.title: Serving a public DNS resolver (DoH + DoT)
items.text:
A dns mapping turns a domain into a standalone, unauthenticated resolver that serves the managed AdGuard Home filter to anyone. This is the self-hosted equivalent of a public resolver such as dns.adguard.com: no TunGuard login, no VPN required, just point a device at your endpoints.

domain add dns.example.com --dns

The mapping exposes exactly two things:

Endpoint Address Purpose DNS-over-HTTPS https://dns.example.com/dns-query DoH, over the standard HTTPS port (DOMAIN_HTTPS_PORT, 443) DNS-over-TLS dns.example.com:853 DoT, on DOMAIN_DOT_PORT (default 853)

The root https://dns.example.com/ serves a TunGuard landing page that shows these two endpoints, so the domain is self-explanatory to anyone who opens it. Only /dns-query is proxied to AdGuard: every other path is a 404, and AdGuard's admin UI and login are never exposed through a DNS mapping.

Requires AdGuard Home

The dns backend needs the managed AdGuard Home instance. It is enabled by default (ADGUARD_ENABLED=true); if it is disabled, domain add ... --dns is rejected and domain status reports AdGuard Home is not running.

items.title: How the endpoints are served
items.text:
DoH reuses the same HTTPS machinery as any other mapping, so it works whether TunGuard terminates TLS itself or an existing webserver does:

  • built-in proxy — the mapping is served directly on DOMAIN_HTTPS_PORT.
  • nginx / Apache / Caddy / Traefik — the generated vhost splits by path: /dns-query is proxied to AdGuard, everything else falls through to the TunGuard landing page on the loopback challenge listener.

DoT is a dedicated listener that TunGuard always binds itself on DOMAIN_DOT_PORT, independent of the webserver:

  • One listener serves every enabled dns mapping, selecting the certificate per-connection by SNI. An unknown or non-DNS hostname is refused.
  • Each accepted TLS connection is tunnelled verbatim to AdGuard's plain DNS listener, so the DNS framing is the client's and AdGuard's, not TunGuard's.
  • The listener starts when the first dns mapping becomes live and stops when the last one is removed or disabled.

Make sure DOMAIN_DOT_PORT (853) is reachable from the internet alongside 80/443, or DoT clients will fail.

One resolver, many domains

Because the DNS backend always points at the single AdGuard Home instance, every dns mapping on a server answers with the same filter and the same blocklists. Multiple domains are useful for branding or redundancy, not for different filtering per-domain.

items.title: Dashboard
items.text: The Domains page lists every mapping with its state, and lets you add, update (including pausing with disable), or remove entries.

items.title: API
items.text:
Endpoint Method Purpose /api/domains GET List mappings plus proxy status /api/domains/status GET Proxy mode, webserver, ports, owner of 80/443 /api/domain/add POST Create a mapping /api/domain/update POST Update a mapping /api/domain/remove POST Delete a mapping /api — All of the above return 409 when the proxy is disabled 
# Behind an existing TRP mapping (referenced by id or unique id prefix)
curl -X POST \
  -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"domain":"app.example.com","backend":"trp","proxy_ref":"3"}' \
  http://localhost:9000/api/domain/add

# Behind a tunneled service
curl -X POST \
  -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"domain":"api.example.com","backend":"wg","target_ip":"10.100.0.2","target_port":8080}' \
  http://localhost:9000/api/domain/add

# A public DoH + DoT resolver
curl -X POST \
  -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"domain":"dns.example.com","backend":"dns"}' \
  http://localhost:9000/api/domain/add

# Pause without deleting
curl -X POST \
  -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"id":"DOMAIN_ID","enabled":false}' \
  http://localhost:9000/api/domain/update

# Remove
curl -X POST \
  -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"id":"DOMAIN_ID"}' \
  http://localhost:9000/api/domain/remove

GET /api/domains/status reports the serving mode so you can tell whether the built-in proxy or an external webserver is active:

{
  "enabled": true,
  "mode": "external",
  "webserver": "nginx",
  "owner_80": "nginx",
  "owner_443": "nginx",
  "http_port": 80,
  "https_port": 443,
  "challenge_port": 8100,
  "dot_port": 853,
  "dot": true,
  "count": 2
}

dot is true while the DoT listener is up (that is, while at least one dns mapping is live), and dot_port is where it listens.

items.title: Console
items.text:
domain list                                     mappings: domain, backend, target, state
domain add app.example.com --trp 3              behind an existing TRP mapping
domain add api.example.com --wg 10.100.0.2 8080 behind a tunneled service
domain add dns.example.com --dns                a public DoH + DoT resolver
domain update app.example.com --disable         pause without deleting
domain remove app.example.com                   by id or domain name

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
Variable Default Description DOMAIN_ENABLED true HTTPS domain proxy. false disables it DOMAIN_HTTP_PORT 80 Public HTTP port for the ACME challenge and redirects DOMAIN_HTTPS_PORT 443 Public HTTPS port of the domain proxy DOMAIN_CHALLENGE_PORT 8100 Loopback port the HTTP-01 challenge answers on DOMAIN_DOT_PORT 853 Public DNS-over-TLS port for dns mappings. 0 disables DoT

Mappings persist in DATA_DIR/domains/domains.json (mode 0600), and certificates plus the ACME account key under DATA_DIR/domains/, which are covered by the usual backup and restore flow.

items.title: Security notes
items.text:
• A public mapping reaches its backend without any added authentication. The services you publish this way are exposed to the internet — protect them in the app, or only map domains you want public.
  • The proxy forwards the request path as-is and preserves the Host header; X-Forwarded-* is set by TunGuard.
  • Certificates are only requested for domains that have a mapping, and unknown Host headers get a 404.
  • A backend that cannot be reached responds 502 bad gateway.
  • A dns mapping is an open resolver by design. Only /dns-query is proxied to AdGuard and AdGuard's admin UI is never reachable through the domain, but anyone who knows the endpoint can query it. The filter applies, and AdGuard's own rate limit does too, so abuse is bounded rather than blocked. Remove the mapping (or disable it) if you no longer want it public.

items.title: End to end: publish a service on a mesh node
items.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
API_KEY="REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_KEY"
API="http://localhost:9000"
field() { python3 -c "import json,sys;print(json.load(sys.stdin)['$1'])"; }

# Enroll a node running the service
ADDED="$(curl -sS -X POST -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" "$API/api/mesh/node/add" \
  -d '{"name":"edge-a"}')"
NODE_ID="$(printf '%s' "$ADDED" | field id)"
echo "run on the device:  tun YOUR_SERVER_IP $(printf '%s' "$ADDED" | field psk)"

# Expose the service on the server through a TRP mapping
PROXY="$(curl -sS -X POST -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" "$API/api/trp/proxy/add" \
  -d "{\"node_id\":\"$NODE_ID\",\"bind_port\":\"\",\"target_port\":\"8022\"}")"
PROXY_ID="$(printf '%s' "$PROXY" | field id)"
echo "tunnel listener:   $(printf '%s' "$PROXY" | field public_url)"

# Put a public HTTPS domain in front of it
curl -sS -X POST -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" "$API/api/domain/add" \
  -d "{\"domain\":\"dashboard.example.com\",\"backend\":\"trp\",\"proxy_ref\":\"$PROXY_ID\"}"

echo "open:  https://dashboard.example.com"

items.title: End to end: publish a public resolver
items.text:
A DNS front is a single mapping. Point the domain's A record at the server, open ports 443 and 853, and add it:

API_KEY="REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_KEY"
API="http://localhost:9000"

curl -sS -X POST -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" "$API/api/domain/add" \
  -d '{"domain":"dns.example.com","backend":"dns"}'

echo "DoH:  https://dns.example.com/dns-query"
echo "DoT:  dns.example.com:853"

Verify it resolves and filters:

# DoH (expect 0.0.0.0 for a blocked ad domain)
curl -s "https://dns.example.com/dns-query?name=doubleclick.net&type=A" \
  -H "accept: application/dns-json"

# DoT
kdig +tls +tls-host=dns.example.com @dns.example.com doubleclick.net

items.title: Install TunGuard
items.text:
Install TunGuard on a fresh Linux server:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TunGuard/get/main/installer.sh | bash

The installer installs and starts TunGuard automatically.

After installation, open the dashboard:

http://YOUR_SERVER_IP:9000

items.title: First Login
items.text:
On a fresh installation, use the default credentials:

  • Username: admin
  • Password: tanguard

You will be required to create new dashboard credentials after your first login. Until you do, /login.html takes over and the rest of the dashboard stays closed.

items.title: Dashboard Setup
items.text:
After logging in, TunGuard is ready to manage your WireGuard server.

The default server configuration is:

  • WireGuard Address: 10.100.0.1/24
  • WireGuard Subnet: 10.100.0.0/24
  • WireGuard Port: 13231
  • Dashboard/API Port: 9000

items.title: Create a Peer
items.text:
Open Peers and create a new peer.

TunGuard generates the peer configuration automatically.

A generated configuration contains:

  • Private Key: The peer's private WireGuard key.
  • Address: The peer's assigned VPN address.
  • DNS: The DNS server used by the peer.
  • Server Public Key: The public key of the TunGuard server.
  • Endpoint: The public address and WireGuard port of the TunGuard server.
  • Allowed IPs: The networks that should be routed through the peer's connection.
  • Persistent Keepalive: Keeps the connection active when the peer is behind NAT.

You can download the configuration, copy it, or scan its QR code using a WireGuard client.

items.title: Peer Address
items.text:
The first peer normally receives:

10.100.0.2/32

Additional peers receive the next available address from the configured VPN subnet.

items.title: Connect the Peer
items.text:
Import the generated configuration into a WireGuard client on the device you want to connect.

The client connects to the TunGuard server using the configured WireGuard endpoint:

YOUR_SERVER_IP:13231

Once connected, the peer appears in the Peers section of the TunGuard dashboard.

items.title: Optional SSH Gateway
items.text:
TunGuard can also provide SSH access to devices connected through the VPN.

Enable the SSH Gateway with:

./tanguard -ssh

The default SSH Gateway port is:

2222

You can then connect to a VPN device through the TunGuard server:

ssh -J admin@YOUR_SERVER_IP:2222 root@10.100.0.2

See SSH Access for the full story: the jump host, the browser SSH terminal, and the built-in ssh client.

items.title: Next steps
items.text: TunGuard also ships a managed AdGuard DNS Filtering instance, a Domains & HTTPS Proxy for publishing internal services, and Policy Groups for isolating devices from each other.

items.title: SSH Access
items.text:
One server becomes the jump host for every machine on your VPN.

TunGuard can act as an SSH jump host and gives you three ways to reach the machines on your VPN: SSH straight through the server with ssh -J, an SSH terminal in the browser from the dashboard, and a built-in ssh client in the dashboard's Terminal.

items.title: The SSH Gateway
items.text:
The SSH Gateway turns TunGuard into an SSH jump host. Enable it with:

sudo ./tanguard -web -ssh

or set SSH_ENABLED=true (the installer's systemd service can also enable it). It listens on SSH_LISTEN, default port 2222.

It authenticates with the same login as the web dashboard — there are no separate SSH credentials. If you change the username or password under Settings → Dashboard Login, SSH access uses the new login immediately.

The gateway's host key is auto-generated (ed25519) at DATA_DIR/ssh_host_key when SSH_KEY_FILE=auto, and is included in backups.

items.title: Reach a peer over the tunnel
items.text:
Jump through the gateway to any connected peer:

ssh -J admin@YOUR_SERVER_IP:2222 root@10.100.0.2
  • admin@YOUR_SERVER_IP:2222 are your TunGuard dashboard credentials and the gateway port — this part authenticates to the gateway.
  • root@10.100.0.2 is the peer you are landing on — this part authenticates to the peer itself, exactly as if the peer's own SSH were public.

You never have to expose SSH on the device to the internet. You can also jump to any other host the server can reach: the gateway forwards whatever TCP host:port you ask it to.

What the gateway forwards

The gateway accepts direct-tcpip forwarding to any host and port the server can reach. That is what makes ssh -J work, and it is intentionally broad — keep the gateway and the dashboard behind a trustworthy network.

Use the console's jump command to print the exact ssh -J line for a peer:

jump laptop

items.title: Connect directly to a peer (no jump)
items.text:
Any peer that runs its own sshd can be reached end to end from the server:

ssh root@10.100.0.2

If the peer has a device label configured you can use it instead of the IP:

ssh laptop

items.title: SSH from the dashboard (Web SSH)
items.text: Next to any online peer on the Peers page there is an SSH button. It opens a browser terminal and connects to the peer over a WebSocket (/api/ws/ssh), prompting you for the peer's own username and password (SSH password auth to the target). The browser session and the peer's SSH are end-to-end encrypted; TunGuard only relays the terminal.

items.title: The built-in SSH client
items.text:
The dashboard Terminal and the SSH gateway's own prompt both include a small ssh client, so you can reach peers (or any host the server can reach) without a second terminal:

ssh root@10.100.0.5                 interactive session to a peer
ssh laptop                          a peer by its device label
ssh -p 2222 -l alice jumpbox        alternate port / login
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 host       use a specific private key
ssh host uptime                     run one remote command and exit
ssh --password s3cret host          non-interactive password (scripts)
  • Ctrl-] detaches an interactive session and returns to the TunGuard prompt.
  • ssh host command streams the remote output and reports the remote exit status.
  • Peers are matched by device label, tunnel address, or key.

items.title: Security notes
items.text:
• The gateway itself accepts password authentication only, using the dashboard login. There is no separate SSH user database.
  • Anything able to reach the API can also request /api/ws/ssh, which opens an interactive shell to the target host — keep the dashboard and API off untrusted networks, and prefer key-based auth on the peers you manage this way.
  • For extra hardening of the peers themselves, consider key-based SSH auth on the devices (the gateway is only one leg of the connection; the second leg authenticates to the peer normally).

items.title: API
items.text: Endpoint Method Purpose /api/ws/ssh GET (WebSocket) Browser SSH session to a peer /api/ws/console GET (WebSocket) The dashboard Terminal
